note: Claim records for the capitalism deep dive. status: drafted = written with sources linked; verified = an independent AI check confirmed the source supports the claim.

events.text: Luca Pacioli publishes the first printed account of double-entry bookkeeping, the accounting method Italian merchants and bankers had developed. Firms still use it today.
The Atlantic slave trade carries about 12.5 million enslaved Africans onto ships; about 10.7 million survive the crossing. Their forced labor grows sugar, tobacco and cotton for world markets.
England charters the East India Company, a trading firm owned by shareholders that later rules much of India with its own army.
The Dutch East India Company (VOC) is founded. It sells shares that can be traded on the Amsterdam exchange, an early model of the modern company and stock market.
To control the nutmeg trade, VOC forces under Jan Pieterszoon Coen conquer the Banda Islands; most of the roughly 15,000 inhabitants are killed, enslaved or driven out.
Tulip bulb prices in the Dutch Republic soar and then collapse. Historian Anne Goldgar found the damage to the wider economy was far smaller than later legends claim.
The Bank of England is founded as a private company to lend money to the government for war. Central banking grows out of arrangements like this.
The South Sea Bubble in Britain and the Mississippi Bubble in France burst after wild speculation in company shares, ruining many investors.
Parliamentary enclosure in England turns shared village land into private farms. Output rises, but many rural families lose access to common land and move to towns for wage work.
After the Battle of Plassey (1757), the East India Company wins the right to collect Bengal’s land revenue (1765), turning a trading company into a government.

Famine kills millions in Bengal; contemporary and later estimates range up to about a third of the population. Historians debate how much Company tax collection and policy worsened a drought-driven crisis.
Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, arguing that the division of labor and free exchange make nations richer, while warning about monopolies and merchants who conspire against the public.

sources.cite: Online Library of Liberty, The Wealth of Nations

events.text: The Industrial Revolution begins in Britain: machines, factories and coal-powered steam engines multiply output, first in cotton textiles.
Eli Whitney’s cotton gin makes it far cheaper to clean short-staple cotton, and slavery spreads rapidly across the US South to grow it.

sources.cite: National Archives, Eli Whitney’s patent for the cotton gin

events.text: About one million enslaved people in the United States are forcibly moved from the upper South to the cotton frontier, many sold away from their families.

sources.cite: Olmstead & Rhode, Explorations in Economic History (2018)
Gilder Lehrman Institute, The domestic slave trade

events.text: David Ricardo explains comparative advantage: two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything.

sources.cite: Online Library of Liberty, Ricardo, Principles

events.text: Britain’s Factory Act bans textile-mill work for children under nine, limits hours for older children, and creates the first factory inspectors.
Britain abolishes slavery in most of its colonies and pays £20 million in compensation, to slave owners, not to the enslaved, who were also forced into years of unpaid “apprenticeship”.

sources.cite: UCL Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery

events.text: About a million people die in the Irish famine and over a million emigrate. Food exports from Ireland continue, and historians debate how far the British government’s free-market relief policy deepened the disaster.
Britain repeals the Corn Laws, which had protected landowners with grain tariffs, a turning point toward free trade.

sources.cite: UK Parliament, The repeal of the Corn Laws

events.text: Marx and Engels publish The Communist Manifesto, the most influential critique of capitalism (see the Marxism–Leninism deep dive).

sources.cite: Marxists Internet Archive, Manifesto of the Communist Party

events.text: British laws let ordinary companies offer limited liability: investors can lose only what they put in. This makes it easier to raise money from many small shareholders.
Japan’s Meiji Restoration begins state-led industrialization: the government builds railways, mills and banks, then sells many to private firms that grow into the zaibatsu.
Under the classical gold standard and falling transport costs, trade and capital flows reach levels the world would not see again until the 1990s.
A financial panic in Vienna and New York starts a long slump in Europe and North America, later called the Long Depression.

In the Congo Free State, owned personally by King Leopold II of Belgium, forced rubber collection enforced by hostage-taking, mutilation and killing causes mass death. Estimates of the toll range from about 1 to 10 million and are disputed.
The US Sherman Antitrust Act outlaws monopolies and cartels that restrain trade.
Max Weber’s The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism argues that religious ideas about work and saving helped shape modern capitalism. The thesis is still debated.
The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York kills 146 garment workers, mostly young immigrant women, behind locked doors. It leads to new safety and labor laws.

sources.cite: Cornell ILR, The Triangle Factory Fire

events.text: Ford introduces the moving assembly line and then the five-dollar day, cutting the price of a car and roughly doubling the usual pay for factory work.

sources.cite: The Henry Ford, Moving assembly line

events.text: The US creates the Federal Reserve after repeated bank panics.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, Federal Reserve Act

events.text: Arthur Pigou’s Economics of Welfare explains externalities, costs such as pollution that fall on people outside a deal, and proposes taxing them.
After the Wall Street crash of October 1929, US output collapses and unemployment rises from about 3% to about 25% in 1933. Thousands of banks fail.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, The Great Depression

events.text: The US Smoot–Hawley Tariff raises import duties; other countries retaliate and world trade shrinks. Economists still debate how much it deepened the Depression.

sources.cite: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

events.text: Drought and years of plowing up native grassland bring the Dust Bowl to the southern Great Plains, driving hundreds of thousands of families off the land.

sources.cite: Library of Congress, Dust Bowl migration

events.text: Roosevelt’s New Deal adds bank deposit insurance, the separation of commercial and investment banking (Glass–Steagall), Social Security, minimum wages and the legal right to join a union.
Keynes’s General Theory argues that economies can stay stuck with high unemployment and that government spending can lift demand.
Ronald Coase asks why firms exist at all, and answers that markets have costs (finding partners, making contracts), so some work is cheaper to organize inside a company.
Joseph Schumpeter describes “creative destruction”: new firms and technologies destroy old ones. He also predicted that capitalism would gradually give way to socialism.
Two rival classics appear: Hayek’s The Road to Serfdom warns that central planning leads to tyranny, and Polanyi’s The Great Transformation argues that unregulated markets tear societies apart.
At Bretton Woods, 44 Allied nations set up the IMF and the World Bank and a system of fixed exchange rates tied to the US dollar and gold.

sources.cite: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

events.text: West Germany’s currency reform and Ludwig Erhard’s lifting of price controls start the “social market economy”, combining markets with strong unions and welfare. Rapid growth follows.

Swedish union economists Gösta Rehn and Rudolf Meidner propose the model behind Sweden’s system: equal pay for equal work across firms, active job retraining and a large welfare state alongside private ownership.

Under Park Chung-hee’s military government, South Korea grows rapidly through state-directed, export-led industrialization: cheap credit for chosen firms (the chaebol), strict export targets, and suppressed labor unions.
Milton Friedman’s New York Times essay argues that a company’s social responsibility is to increase its profits within the rules of the game.
President Nixon ends the dollar’s convertibility into gold, ending the Bretton Woods system.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, Nixon ends convertibility

events.text: Two oil shocks and “stagflation” (high inflation with high unemployment) undermine faith in Keynesian management and open the way for market-oriented reforms.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, The Great Inflation

events.text: After the 1973 military coup in Chile, economists trained in Chicago (the “Chicago Boys”) privatize, cut tariffs and create private pensions. Growth and poverty reduction follow, along with a 1982 crash, high inequality, and a dictatorship that killed and tortured thousands.

sources.cite: Cato Journal, The Fall of Chile (2020)
Museo de la Memoria y los Derechos Humanos (Chile)

events.text: China begins “reform and opening up”: farm families may sell surplus crops, special economic zones welcome foreign firms, and markets slowly spread under Communist Party rule.
Britain under Margaret Thatcher and the US under Ronald Reagan cut top tax rates, curb union power and (in Britain) privatize state industries.
Economist John Williamson names the “Washington Consensus”: ten market-oriented policies promoted by the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury.

sources.cite: Peterson Institute, What Washington Means by Policy Reform

events.text: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis, India’s Finance Minister Manmohan Singh abolishes most industrial licensing, cuts tariffs and opens to foreign investment.

Russia’s rapid transition (“shock therapy”, voucher privatization, the 1995 loans-for-shares deals that created billionaire oligarchs) coincides with a deep slump, a 1998 default and a sharp fall in male life expectancy. Causes of the death spike are debated.

sources.cite: Brainerd & Cutler, Journal of Economic Perspectives (2005)

events.text: The Asian financial crisis hits Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea after a rush of short-term foreign money reverses.

sources.cite: Federal Reserve History, Asian financial crisis

events.text: China joins the World Trade Organization. Research later finds the resulting surge of imports explains about a quarter of the fall in US manufacturing jobs from 1990 to 2007, with lasting local damage.

sources.cite: Autor, Dorn & Hanson, American Economic Review (2013)

events.text: The US housing bubble bursts; Lehman Brothers fails on 15 September 2008 and a global financial crisis follows. The official US inquiry (2011) concluded the crisis was avoidable, but its members split over the causes.
The Rana Plaza garment factory building collapses in Bangladesh, killing 1,134 workers who made clothes for global brands. It leads to a binding safety accord.

sources.cite: International Labour Organization, The Rana Plaza accident and its aftermath

events.text: Thomas Piketty’s Capital in the Twenty-First Century argues that wealth tends to concentrate when returns on capital outpace growth. Other economists dispute the data and the theory.

sources.cite: Harvard University Press, Capital in the Twenty-First Century

events.text: The US Business Roundtable says companies should serve customers, workers, suppliers and communities as well as shareholders, a shift away from the Friedman view. Critics doubt behavior changed.

sources.cite: Business Roundtable, Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation

events.text: A sharp scholarly dispute: Sullivan and Hickel argue that the rise of capitalism made welfare worse for centuries; Rutar and others reply that poverty was common before capitalism and that colonialism is not the same thing as capitalism.
The World Bank raises its extreme-poverty line to $3.00 a day. By that measure about 830 million people remain extremely poor, down from about 2.3 billion in 1990.

sources.cite: World Bank, June 2025 update to global poverty lines

events.text: The World Inequality Report 2026 estimates that the richest 10% own about three-quarters of the world’s wealth and the poorest half about 2%.
The economics Nobel goes to Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson for research on how institutions shaped by colonization explain why some nations are richer than others.
The economics Nobel goes to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for explaining growth driven by innovation and creative destruction.
US government data show that about one in five new business establishments closes within its first year and about half within five years.

sources.cite: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, The Economics Daily

people.name: Ibn Khaldun
people.text: Argued in the Muqaddimah that high taxes eventually shrink the economy and that labor creates value, ideas later economists rediscovered.

people.name: Adam Smith
people.text: Explained the division of labor and the “invisible hand” of markets, but also attacked monopolies and cared about the poor.

people.name: David Ricardo
people.text: Showed how countries gain from trade through comparative advantage; a successful stockbroker and member of Parliament.

people.name: John Stuart Mill
people.text: Defended free markets and liberty but supported worker cooperatives, inheritance taxes and women’s rights.

people.name: Karl Marx
people.text: The most influential critic of capitalism; argued that profit comes from unpaid labor and that the system would end in crisis.

people.name: Andrew Carnegie
people.text: Built a steel empire through ruthless cost-cutting and fought unions (the 1892 Homestead strike), then gave away most of his fortune to libraries and universities.

people.name: Mary Harris Jones (“Mother Jones”)
people.text: Labor organizer for miners and child workers; the nickname came from the workers she organized, who called her “mother”.

people.name: Max Weber
people.text: Linked the spirit of capitalism to Protestant ideas about work and saving, and studied bureaucracy and the modern state.

people.name: Henry Ford
people.text: Made cars affordable with the moving assembly line and high wages; also published antisemitic propaganda in his newspaper.

people.name: Frances Perkins
people.text: First woman in a US cabinet; as Labor Secretary she shaped Social Security, the minimum wage and limits on child labor.

sources.cite: US Department of Labor, Frances Perkins

people.name: John Maynard Keynes
people.text: Argued that governments must manage demand to avoid mass unemployment; helped design the Bretton Woods system.

people.name: Joseph Schumpeter
people.text: Described entrepreneurs and “creative destruction” as the engine of capitalism.

people.name: Karl Polanyi
people.text: Argued that turning land, labor and money into market goods provokes society to protect itself.

people.name: Friedrich Hayek
people.text: Argued that prices carry knowledge no planner could gather; Nobel Prize 1974.

people.name: Raúl Prebisch
people.text: Argued that poorer countries exporting raw materials lose out in trade with industrial countries, inspiring import-substitution policies across Latin America.

people.name: Ludwig Erhard
people.text: Launched West Germany’s social market economy in 1948 and later became chancellor.

people.name: Milton Friedman
people.text: Argued for free markets and steady money growth; Nobel Prize 1976. His students advised Chile’s military government.

people.name: Ronald Coase
people.text: Explained why firms exist and how property rights can settle conflicts like pollution; Nobel Prize 1991.

people.name: Park Chung-hee
people.text: Military ruler who drove export-led industrialization while repressing opposition and unions.

people.name: Deng Xiaoping
people.text: Led China’s market reforms after 1978 while keeping one-party rule; ordered the 1989 Tiananmen crackdown.

people.name: Elinor Ostrom
people.text: Showed that communities often manage shared resources well without either state control or privatization; Nobel Prize 2009.

people.name: Amartya Sen
people.text: Showed that famines come from people losing the means to buy food, not only from shortage; Nobel Prize 1998.

people.name: Muhammad Yunus
people.text: Founded Grameen Bank to make small loans to poor borrowers, mostly women; Nobel Peace Prize 2006. The results of microcredit are debated.

people.name: Manmohan Singh
people.text: As finance minister in 1991 he opened India’s economy; later prime minister from 2004 to 2014.

people.name: Walter Rodney
people.text: Argued in How Europe Underdeveloped Africa that colonial capitalism drained Africa’s wealth; assassinated in Guyana in 1980.

people.name: Hernando de Soto
people.text: Argued that the poor hold vast assets they cannot use as capital because they lack legal property titles.

people.name: Deirdre McCloskey
people.text: Argues that the great enrichment came mostly from new respect for ordinary business people and innovation, not from trade or exploitation.

sources.cite: University of Illinois Chicago, Deirdre McCloskey

people.name: Ha-Joon Chang
people.text: Argues that rich countries grew rich using protection and state support, then told poorer countries not to.

sources.cite: SOAS University of London, Ha-Joon Chang

people.name: Thomas Piketty
people.text: Built long-run data on income and wealth inequality and argues for global wealth taxes.

sources.cite: Paris School of Economics, Thomas Piketty
